title: Local profit-tax rises squeeze cash and weaken credit quality at small Portuguese firms
summary: João B. Duarte and Afonso S. Moura follow the same Portuguese companies from the year their municipality raises its corporate surtax into the subsequent years of borrowing, investment and employment. A typical increase of 0.88 percentage points in the statutory surtax raises the effective tax rate by 0.76 points. Firms draw down liquidity and take on debt, initially at short maturities. Distress shows up later in bank records, alongside lower employment and measured productivity. This sequence makes the tax change relevant to credit analysis even when the initial rise in corporate debt appears small relative to the balance sheet.

Portugal’s 278 mainland municipalities set a surtax of up to 1.5% on a nationally defined corporate profit base. The authors match annual accounts to Banco de Portugal’s Central Credit Registry and compare private non-financial firms with more than one employee in municipalities that raised the rate with comparable firms elsewhere. They exploit staggered changes observed from 2009 to 2021. The baseline restricts municipalities to those with at most one change and excludes recent or imminent changes from the control group. Comparisons account for common district and industry shocks in each year. Municipal gross value added does not predict a rate increase in Table 2. The design still assumes otherwise similar trajectories for affected and comparison firms, since municipalities choose their own rates.

Figures 3 and 4 show why a higher leverage ratio needs interpretation. Net financial debt rises by about 7% immediately, while fixed assets decline more slowly. Leverage increases around 0.85 percentage points on impact and 1.5 points after three years. Liquidity falls about 0.95 points after four years. Supplier payables also rise relative to the cost of goods sold, consistent with slower payment. The implicit interest rate rises by about 0.47 points in the first year after the increase. Short-term borrowing rises faster than longer-term borrowing, and after four years the share of firms carrying a non-performing loan is around 1.4 percentage points higher (Figures 5 and 6).

Operating performance deteriorates as well. Three years after the increase, estimated productivity is about 2.5% lower. Employment falls about 2% and total labour costs about 3%, suggesting part of the burden reaches workers through compensation per worker as well as jobs. In Table 3, smaller firms are the group where falling liquidity and higher leverage coincide. Larger firms show no statistically significant response in these financial measures. Previously profitable firms also respond more strongly. This pattern supports the authors’ interpretation that borrowing helps cover cash shortages. The analysis cannot apportion the subsequent loss of activity between higher taxes directly and tighter external finance.

Table 4 examines two different ways a firm can disappear from local statistics. The estimated probability of leaving the firm panel the following year rises by 2.2 percentage points. The probability of changing the registered headquarters municipality rises by 7.7 points, with a stronger relocation response for companies operating several establishments. Neighbouring municipalities in the same district gain a small number of firms, but Figure 8 finds little durable change in their aggregate value added. A headquarters move can therefore change which authority records a company while saying little about where its workers, production and credit exposures end up. For a lender or local policymaker, the movement in firm registrations and the deterioration observed in surviving borrowers answer different questions.

questions.question: How much of the decline in employment is transmitted through tighter bank credit?
questions.detail: Compare similarly exposed borrowers with different amounts of unused committed credit before their municipality voted, and follow borrowing terms, supplier payments and employment through the same horizons. If firms with ample pre-existing credit lose fewer jobs despite a similar tax bill, that would help distinguish the financing channel from the direct effect of a lower return on production. Bank credit-register data matched to the tax filings would help lenders identify the vulnerable borrowers.

questions.question: Are apparent gains in firm numbers across the municipal border accompanied by any movement of workers or productive assets?
questions.detail: Link changes of headquarters to establishment-level payroll, fixed investment and sales. Comparing firms that already operated on both sides of the border with single-establishment movers would help explain why Figure 8 detects more registrations in neighbouring municipalities yet little increase in value added. Establishment registers and municipal tax receipts would clarify whether relocation changes the underlying economic exposure of local lenders.

questions.question: How much credit deterioration disappears from view when a treated firm exits?
questions.detail: Track the final loan status and repayment or write-off of departing borrowers, alongside a fixed cohort of continuing firms. Comparing measures based on the original borrower cohort with the four-year incidence in Figure 6 would show whether changes in the composition of surviving firms conceal more of the risk borne by banks, or instead concentrate risk within the surviving sample. The credit register and insolvency records would supply the relevant borrower histories for evaluating expected credit losses.

limitation: The empirical design relies on comparable counterfactual trends across municipalities. The data identify a registered headquarters move and exit from the firm panel, while the analysis does not identify the causal share of lost activity attributable to financing constraints.
